How to read this

What is the "resting level"?

While a pump runs, the water near the well is pulled down, so readings taken during pumping look deeper than the groundwater really is. We use the level recorded when a pump starts after at least 12 hours of rest. That is the closest we get to the true groundwater level, and it is what we forecast.

Why give a range instead of one number?

Nobody can know next month's water level exactly. The range is built from how far off our past forecasts actually were: 80% of the time, the real level landed inside it. A wide range is honest, not a failure.

Where does the forecast come from?

It blends two views. One is the well's recent trend. The other is a model of how this well responds to its own pumping and to Bengaluru rainfall over the past weeks. For future weeks we assume pumping continues at its recent average and rainfall is typical for the season. What moves the water →

How good is it, overall?

Across 495 wells and 8 test dates, the typical error was about 0.3 m one week ahead and 1.3 m on average twelve weeks ahead, half the error of assuming nothing changes. See the full accuracy check →

Is this real data?

This page uses a digital twin: a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a full year (Aug 2025 – Jul 2026). The simulation's well IDs do not correspond to the wells in the Stage 1 vendor export. No real water-level measurement has been used yet; repeating this on real long-term records is the next step. What we need →

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
